name: Sagar Uniyal
role: Software engineer at a cross-border payments & digital-wallet company; builds AI agents and developer tools on the side and at work
day_job_themes: Cross-border remittance integrations with banks in Pakistan, Bangladesh and the UAE (SOAP and REST payout partners)
An Incentive Engine: promo campaigns with segment targeting and a reserve -> consume -> release budget lifecycle
User segmentation on a CDC pipeline (Debezium -> Kafka -> ClickHouse)
Notification engine, RBAC refactor, maker-checker refund flows, multi-region rollouts

projects.name: ACE 2.0
projects.one_liner: GraphRAG over a company's whole git history, rebuilt in Go as a single 17MB static binary
projects.story: Rewrote a Python knowledge service in Go with pure-Go SQLite (no cgo, no JVM) so it ships with scp. People <-> commits <-> files graph plus lexical and vector retrieval. Found that our first retriever cited off-topic sources because lexical scoring had no IDF and dropped repeated tokens; fixing it changed answer quality more than any model upgrade.

projects.name: AMP (Agent Message Protocol)
projects.one_liner: A prompt-native protocol for agents to talk to each other, HMAC-signed per agent
projects.story: Every message is human-readable text an LLM can write and parse, inside a JSON envelope signed with a per-agent secret, so even a compromised hub can't forge an agent's message. Built an Orchestrator on it that knows everyone's in-flight changes.

projects.name: Voice payments on smart glasses
projects.one_liner: Sending money by voice through Ray-Ban Meta glasses used as a plain Bluetooth headset
projects.story: The glasses had no SDK I could use, so I treated them as a Bluetooth headset: audio -> local whisper.cpp -> intent -> exact payee match -> signed mandate -> device-key signature -> append-only ledger. The hard part wasn't speech, it was payee disambiguation: similar names collided until I added an admission step that demanded full names on ambiguity.

projects.name: Support assistant with its own intent model
projects.one_liner: Own small intent classifier (ONNX on CPU) in front of the LLM, with guardrails
projects.story: Instead of sending every customer message to an LLM, trained a small intent model that runs on CPU. Went through 24 versions; blind-set accuracy reached 93.7% with a 95% target, and the LLM is only called where it adds value. Refund rules, scope walls and a phrase bank sit around it.

projects.name: TenAI Terminal
projects.one_liner: A multi-user terminal of coding agents with an intent gate and a hash-chained audit ledger
projects.story: Engineers sign in with an email OTP and talk to a codebase-aware agent in its own git worktree. An intent gate refuses anything that isn't about code before a single token is spent. Agents can't push: the server squashes the session into one commit, pushes a branch and opens an MR, and a human merges. Every decision lands in a SHA-256 hash-chained ledger.

projects.name: Trading AI
projects.one_liner: Multi-agent trading research platform where the Risk agent has veto power
projects.story: Market, quant, news, strategy, critic, risk and portfolio agents with typed schemas. Python does all the math; the LLM only reasons. The critic challenges every thesis, the risk agent can veto, live execution is off by default (paper trading only), and a strategy is only promoted after backtest, walk-forward, out-of-sample, robustness and paper evaluation. Never treat LLM confidence as a probability.

projects.name: Creator OS
projects.one_liner: An autonomous faceless-media pipeline: research -> script -> voice -> video -> captions
projects.story: A director agent plans each video and even picks the caption font that fits the niche and mood. Mock and real media providers sit behind one interface, so the whole loop is testable without spending money.

projects.name: Venture Lab
projects.one_liner: 10 vertical-AI micro-SaaS apps built overnight by agents, with a live command center
projects.story: Wrote a master plan, then let agents build ten vertical AI web apps overnight while a command center showed progress live. The lesson: the plan and the acceptance checks mattered far more than the prompts.

projects.name: TeamLens
projects.one_liner: Ask-anything agent for an engineering org, grounded in real git history
projects.story: Claude with tools that query commits, owners and activity, not a vector blob. It answers 'who should I ask about refunds' and surfaces bus-factor-1 modules. Prompt caching on the system prompt makes repeat questions cheap.

projects.name: Vantage
projects.one_liner: A change-collision radar for multi-agent software delivery
projects.story: Before anyone merges, it shows who else is already changing the same files, symbols, tables or endpoints. Planner -> executor -> tester -> merger agents run on a continuously built code graph, offline-first.

projects.name: QA automation studio
projects.one_liner: A live Claude agent that drives web apps and an Android emulator to test releases
projects.story: Give it the release scope and it plans and executes test journeys on web and emulator, recording evidence, so QA spends time on judgment instead of clicking.

projects.name: Self-hosted attack-surface & brand monitoring
projects.one_liner: External attack surface management plus brand-impersonation monitoring, self-hosted
projects.story: Stood up an open-source EASM stack for the company, then added brand protection: lookalike domains, fake social profiles and news mentions, with a strict rule that nothing is kept without evidence.

projects.name: Production debugging war stories
projects.story: Users got the same success notification repeatedly: a stale Kafka dedupe key. Settlement legs stuck in PENDING: a poller regex still matched the old leg names after a rename. A dev API that timed out on every request: a pending ALTER TABLE holding a metadata lock that blocked all reads. Budgets not consumed after discounted payments: apply() re-scanned campaigns instead of targeting the quoted one.

voice: Builder who ships. Concrete, specific, a little playful. Shows the real system and the real mistake, not hype. Short lines, no corporate filler.
audience: Engineers, engineering leaders, AI builders, fintech people, recruiters
